passages.title: Can Seaweed Help Our Planet?
lines: When people think about ways to fight climate change, they often imagine solar panels or electric cars.
However, some scientists believe that one of the most useful tools may be growing quietly in the sea: seaweed.
Like trees on land, seaweed takes in carbon dioxide as it grows.
Some types grow extremely fast, up to half a meter in a single day.
Because of this, large seaweed farms could remove a lot of carbon dioxide in a short time.
Seaweed also gives food and shelter to many small fish and other sea creatures.
In some coastal areas, farmers have started growing seaweed together with shellfish such as oysters.
The shellfish help clean the water, and the seaweed helps keep the water healthy for the shellfish.
As a result, both grow better than they would on their own.
Seaweed can be used in many ways, too.
It is eaten in soups and salads. It can also be turned into animal food, fertilizer, and even packaging that breaks down naturally.
On the other hand, experts warn that seaweed farming is not a perfect solution.
If farms become too large, they may block sunlight and harm other ocean life.
Also, when seaweed dies and sinks, scientists are not yet sure how long the carbon stays at the bottom of the sea.
For now, most researchers agree that seaweed can be part of the answer, but not the whole answer.
Reducing the amount of carbon dioxide we produce is still the most important step.

passages.title: Young Inventors Challenge at Riverside Science Museum
lines: Do you have an idea that could make life a little easier? Join the Young Inventors Challenge!
Who can enter: Students in grades 4 to 8, alone or in teams of up to three.
Theme: An invention that solves a small problem in everyday life.
How to enter: Send a drawing of your invention and a short explanation (no more than 200 words) by March 10.
Entries can be sent by mail or handed in at the museum's front desk.
Rule 1: Inventions must be your own idea. Adults may help you find materials, but they must not build any part of the invention for you.
Rule 2: Inventions may use up to three batteries. No fire or sharp tools may be used during the final show.
Final show: Ten finalists will be invited to show their inventions at the museum on April 5.
Prizes: The winner will receive a one-year family pass to the museum. All finalists will receive a certificate.
Special prize: Visitors to the final show will vote for the "People's Choice" award.
Questions? Please ask at the front desk.

passages.title: The Lighthouse Interview
lines: For her class project on "jobs of the past," Mia decided to interview Mr. Hughes, who had been a lighthouse keeper for thirty years.
She prepared ten questions the night before and practiced asking them in front of the mirror.
When she arrived at his house by the harbor, however, she was so nervous that she forgot to take out her notebook.
Mr. Hughes smiled and offered her a cup of warm tea.
"Let's just chat first," he said. "The questions can wait."
He told her about windy nights at the lighthouse. On those nights, he climbed its 120 steps again and again to keep the light shining.
He also described the calm mornings when dolphins swam past the rocks below.
Mia became so interested that she stopped worrying and began asking questions that were not on her list.
"Did you ever feel lonely?" she asked.
"Sometimes," he answered. "But I knew that ships far away were counting on me. That made me feel connected to people I would never meet."
When she got home, Mia realized she had used only two of her ten prepared questions.
At first she was worried, but when her report came back, her teacher had written, "The best interviews feel like real conversations. This report is full of life!"
Mia decided to send Mr. Hughes a copy of her report along with a thank-you letter.

prompts.askEn: Some people say students should spend one day a month learning outside the classroom, for example at farms, museums, or local shops. Do you agree? Why or why not?

prompts.sample: I agree with this idea. I think students can learn a lot by seeing things with their own eyes. Also, it is a good chance to talk with people in our town. Because the experience is real, we will probably remember it much longer than a lesson in the classroom.

prompts.askEn: That's interesting. Can you give me an example of something students could learn on one of those days?
prompts.askJa: おもしろいね。そういう 日に どんな ことを 学べそうか、例を ひとつ 教えて。

writing.promptEn: QUESTION: Should every town have a children's council that can suggest ideas to the mayor? Write your opinion with two reasons in 80-100 words.
writing.promptJa: しつもん: どの 町にも、市長に アイデアを 提案できる「こども会議」が あるべきだと 思いますか？ 意見と 理由を 2つ、80〜100 語の 英語で 書きましょう。
writing.sample: I think every town should have a children's council. First, children notice problems that adults often miss. For example, many children walk to school, so they know which roads are dangerous. If they can tell the mayor, the town can become safer for everyone. Second, a council teaches children how to discuss ideas and respect different opinions. These skills will be useful in the future. Some people may say children are too young to make decisions. However, they only need to suggest ideas, not decide everything. For these reasons, children's councils are a good idea.
